summary: Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who studied at the University of Leipzig under Ernst Windisch (Dr. phil. 1897). He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1919) before serving as professor of Indian philology at Leipzig (1919–1937).

Indologist Johannes Klatt studied at Humboldt University of Berlin under Albrecht Weber and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg under August Friedrich Pott (PhD ~1873). From 1872, he worked at the Royal Library of Berlin, becoming librarian in 1889.

Johannes Lohmann worked in linguistics and philosophy, completing a Ph.D. at Berlin (1923) and habilitating under Wilhelm Schulze (~1928). He held professorships at the University of Rostock (1940) and the University of Freiburg (1943; ordinary professor 1949–1963).
Indologist Johannes Mehlig studied under Friedrich Weller (~1948–1953) and Paul Thieme (~1953–1958).

Johannes Nobel specialized in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, earning his PhD (1911) under Heinrich Lüders at Berlin. After teaching in Berlin, he held the chair of Indology at the University of Marburg from 1928 to 1955.

Johannes Rahder studied at Leiden and Utrecht (Ph.D. under Willem Caland), also studying under Louis de La Vallée Poussin. He held chairs at Utrecht (1929–1931), Leiden (1931–1946), and was a professor at Yale University (1947–1965).
Johannes Reinoud Abraham Loman was an Indologist who earned his PhD at the University of Amsterdam under Adriaan Scharpé in 1956. He held a post at Leiden University from 1958 to 1973.

Johannes Schmidt studied at Bonn, Jena (PhD under August Schleicher), and Berlin. He was a professor of comparative linguistics and Sanskrit at the University of Graz (1873–1876) before becoming a professor at Humboldt University of Berlin in 1876.

Johannes Schneider studied at the University of Marburg (Magister 1992). Active in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies, he held posts at Freie Universität Berlin, the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and became apl. Professor at Munich in 2014.

Johannes Schubert studied at Leipzig and Berlin (Ph.D. 1928). Active in Tibetology and Sinology, he worked at the Leipzig University Library (1928–1954) and held professorships and directorships at the University of Leipzig from 1934 to 1965.

Johannes Toepffer was a scholar in history, archaeology, and linguistics who studied at the University of Tartu under Leo Meyer (~1878–1881) and under Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff. He held a post at the University of Basel (~1891–1895).

John A. Ardussi studied under Turrell V. Wylie and earned a PhD from the Australian National University. A specialist in Tibetology and history/archaeology, he has held posts with CNRS and as Senior Research Fellow at the University of Virginia.

John Alexander Corrie Boswell was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology who served as a colonial civil servant in the Madras Civil Service (1855–1871) and the Indian Civil Service (~1856–1872).

John Alexander Jorgensen completed an MA at the Australian National University under Kenneth H. J. Gardiner in 1979. He has held academic posts at ANU and Griffith University, working in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology.

John Alexander Stewart studied at the University of Aberdeen (~1899–1903) and served in the Indian Civil Service (~1905–1933). He later worked in linguistics as Reader in Burmese at the University of London and SOAS (~1933–1948).

Indologist and historian John Allan studied at Edinburgh and Leipzig. He was Deputy Keeper of Coins and Medals at the British Museum (1924–1949) and lectured in Sanskrit at UCL (1907–1917), SOAS (1920–1922), and Edinburgh (1949–1955).

John Anderson earned an M.D. from the University of Edinburgh (~1862). He served as Professor of Natural History at Free Church College, Curator/Supervisor of the Indian Museum in Kolkata (1865–1886), and Professor of Comparative Anatomy at Calcutta Medical College.
John Archibald Boyle studied at Radley College until 1858 and worked in Indology while serving in the Madras Civil Service from 1865.

John Avery studied at Amherst, Yale under William Dwight Whitney, Berlin, and Tübingen. Working in Indology and linguistics, he was Professor of Greek at Grinnell College (1870–1877) and Bowdoin College (1877–1887).
John B. Carman is an Indologist and religious studies scholar who served as Director of the Center for the Study of World Religions at Harvard University (attested 1999).
